Jean-Paul Sartre. A French philosopher from 1905 to 1980 who became the public face of existentialism in the mid-twentieth century. His radical claim—existence precedes essence—reversed millennia of philosophy. He wrote dense theoretical works like Being and Nothingness and Critique of Dialectical Reason, and also accessible novels like Nausea that made philosophy urgent and personal. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature but refused it. His partnership with Simone de Beauvoir and his philosophical rivalry with Albert Camus defined European intellectual life during the Cold War.

Existence precedes essence is Sartre's central claim. Unlike manufactured objects—a knife has an essence, its design and purpose, before it exists—humans exist first and then create their essence through choices and actions. We are condemned to be free. We must choose our values and make ourselves. Sartre developed phenomenology as his philosophical method: describing the structure of conscious experience from the first-person perspective. Being and Nothingness, published in 1943, is a massive phenomenological ontology of consciousness, freedom, and nothingness.

Bad faith, in French mauvaise foi, is Sartre's term for the human tendency to deny freedom and responsibility by pretending we have no choice. A waiter who entirely identifies with his role, a woman who pretends not to recognize sexual advances, a person who says "I had no choice"—all exemplify bad faith. Recognizing bad faith requires acknowledging the anxiety of radical freedom. We cannot escape the burden of choice.

Sartre was a committed political activist, especially against colonialism and fascism. He supported Marxism and engaged in public controversy. He lived in cafés like the Café de Flore, where intellectuals gathered, making philosophy a public practice. His relationship with Simone de Beauvoir was lifelong and productive. They were philosophical partners and lovers who maintained an open relationship, radically unconventional for the era. Her book The Second Sex applied existentialism to gender and became foundational to feminism.

Consciousness, for Sartre, is nothingness. Unlike objects, consciousness has no fixed essence. It is pure negation, freedom, and transcendence. This made consciousness the ground of freedom but also the source of anguish—we cannot escape the burden of choice. In 1952, Sartre's philosophical rivalry with Albert Camus came to a head over Marxism and commitment. Camus rejected Marxism as deterministic and a betrayal of individual freedom. Sartre defended it as the only viable politics. Their public break symbolized deeper tensions between existentialism and absurdism.

Later in life, Sartre revised his philosophy. Critique of Dialectical Reason attempted to reconcile existentialism with Marxism and to account for how historical structures constrain freedom—a move toward what he called existential Marxism.
